result: Curtaining propensity was systematically evaluated across four plasma gases (argon, xenon, nitrogen, oxygen) at three ion currents (high, medium, low) and two voltages (30 and 20 kV). Nitrogen and oxygen exhibited the greatest curtaining propensity, while argon and xenon produced the smoothest surfaces with curtaining propensity under 10% at low currents (~0.2 nA). Argon showed lower curtaining than xenon at higher currents. No temporal accumulation of curtaining was observed during automated serial pFIB/SEM.
evaluation: Claims C34-C41 provide a comprehensive experimental design with quantitative curtaining scores across multiple conditions (gases, currents, voltages) supported by figures. The trend toward greater curtaining at high currents (C35), the exception for nitrogen at 20 kV (C36), and the comparative performance of different gases (C37-C40) are all data-driven observations. The lack of temporal curtaining accumulation (C41) demonstrates stability over acquisition time.

result: Plasma ion beam probe sizes were characterized and found to be considerably larger than Ga-based sources for corresponding currents. At 30 kV, argon produced the smallest probe sizes, while xenon, nitrogen, and oxygen were similar. At 20 kV, argon and xenon showed early plateau behavior while oxygen and nitrogen increased linearly with current.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by direct measurements with figures (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and citation to Ga+ source comparison. The quantitative characterization of probe sizes across different gases and voltages provides essential technical parameters for understanding milling resolution capabilities.

result: Imaging parameters were optimized for cryo-serial pFIB/SEM. A 50 nm milling step was chosen as a compromise between workflow and electron interaction depth (estimated 30 nm for biological polymers, 90 nm for silver beads in cells). Optimal imaging parameters were 1.1-1.2 kV with 6.3-13 pA current, using 100 ns dwell time and 50-100 line integration.
evaluation: Claims C45-C49 describe the rationale for parameter selection supported by citations (C46, C47) and empirical optimization (C48, C49). The compromise between milling step size and electron interaction depth is well-justified, and the imaging parameters are specific and reproducible.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of plunge-frozen HeLa cells (500 slices) revealed various membranous compartments including nucleus, ER, mitochondria, and mitochondrial cristae. Two centrosomes with pairs of centrioles were observed, with centrosome separation of ~1.2 µm consistent with prophase. Centriole spacing was 543 nm in one centrosome and 1561 nm in the other, a heterogeneity consistent with dividing cells. Spindle microtubules were not observed.
evaluation: Claims C50-C56 provide detailed structural observations with quantitative measurements supported by figures and citations. The identification of cell cycle stage (prophase) based on centrosome separation (C53) is supported by citation, and the heterogeneity in centriole spacing (C54-C55) is contextualized with prior work. The absence of spindle microtubules (C56) is noted as a negative observation.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of vitrified mouse brain tissue (844.4 µm³ volume) enabled observation of diverse cell types including neurons and oligodendrocytes. Myelinated neurons ranged from ~0.53 to ~2.8 µm in diameter (mean 1.02±0.73 µm). Approximately 87 mitochondria were observed with visible cristae. Synaptic junctions were visualized with pre-synaptic vesicles (20-30 nm diameter), with ~184 vesicles in Synapse I and ~98 in Synapse II. Post-synaptic densities were visible, and synaptic morphologies were diverse, consistent with previous studies.
evaluation: Claims C57-C68 provide comprehensive structural characterization of brain tissue with quantitative measurements of volumes, cell dimensions, organelle counts, and synaptic features. The observations are supported by figures and citations (C66, C68). The diversity in synaptic morphology is appropriately contextualized with prior work.

result: Imaging at 90° to the milled surface significantly improved image quality compared to 52° imaging. SEM imaging at 52° produced a global resolution of 76±19 nm, while 90° imaging achieved 47±7 nm resolution. The outer membrane of bacteria exemplified improved contrast at 90°. Manual optimization of focus at 52° improved resolution, but 90° imaging still yielded more detail and higher contrast due to differences in electron collection efficiency.
evaluation: Claims C69-C74 provide quantitative resolution measurements using FRC analysis supported by figures. The comparison between imaging angles is systematic with controlled parameters, and the physical basis for improved contrast at 90° is supported by citation (C74). The improvement is both visually apparent and quantitatively measured.

result: Stage movement for 90° imaging introduced minimal drift. XY shift was 52±38 nm without stage movement and 96±71 nm with stage movement (twofold increase but <1% of FOV). Z-drift was minimal with observed milling steps of 48.1±1.4 nm (no stage movement) and 48.9±4 nm (stage movement) for a targeted 50 nm step, confirming the targeted Z step is achievable under cryogenic conditions.
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 provide quantitative measurements of drift and milling precision supported by figures and citation. The small magnitude of drift relative to FOV (C76) and the accuracy of Z-step control (C77-C79) demonstrate the technical feasibility of the 90° imaging approach with stage movement.

result: The depth of field at both 1 and 2 kV imaging energy was found to be ~20 µm. Using a 50 nm slice thickness, focus correction would be needed after approximately 400 slices.
evaluation: Claims C80-C81 provide a quantitative measurement of depth of field supported by a figure, with C81 being a straightforward calculation based on C80. This information is relevant for determining when autofocus corrections are needed during long acquisition runs.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of plunge-frozen R. rubrum revealed minimal subcellular artifacts with clear visualization of lipid droplets and inner/outer membranes (30-80 nm apart). Both developing and mature chromatophores (~30-60 nm diameter) were observed, with nascent chromatophores budding from the inner membrane unambiguously discerned—a visualization not previously achieved at this scale. In eight segmented cells, 2772 mature and 84 nascent chromatophores were observed, with nascent chromatophores unevenly distributed (one cell with ~12% nascent, most with few or none). Data collection was accomplished in 2.5 hr in an automated manner.
evaluation: Claims C82-C92 provide detailed structural observations of R. rubrum with quantitative counts and size measurements supported by figures and citations. The observation of nascent chromatophore budding (C86-C87) is claimed as novel, and the uneven distribution across cells (C90-C91) demonstrates the value of large-volume imaging for capturing rare events (C92). The automated acquisition time (C84) demonstrates practical feasibility.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of plunge-frozen Vero cells using nitrogen plasma severely limited automation (46 slices vs. 500 for HeLa) after seven previous attempts. Despite limitations, subcellular structures were clearly visible including 138 NPCs and characterized mitochondrial networks (isolated, small networks, large networks). Volumes of mitochondria, ER, and LDs were calculated, with 26 LD-to-ER contacts and 48 mitochondria-to-ER MCS identified. Both types of MCS had similar volumes (1-5 × 10⁻³ µm³) and Gaussian distributions, suggesting a limit in ER tracking and contact with organelles.
evaluation: Claims C93-C102 document both the technical challenges with nitrogen plasma (C94-C95) and the biological insights obtained despite these limitations. The quantitative analysis of organelle volumes and membrane contact sites (C99-C101) is supported by figures and citations. The interpretation about ER contact limits (C102) is a reasonable inference from the observed similarity in MCS distributions.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM of fixed (4% paraformaldehyde) and vitrified mouse heart tissue revealed sarcomere-containing regions (myofibrils) between mitochondrial columns. Z-disc, I-band, A-bands, and putative M-line were visible with average sarcomere length of 1.68 µm (SD=0.03, N=34). One nucleus with NPCs and hetero/euchromatin regions was observed, along with blood vessels identified by endothelial cells and red blood cells. In the 2698.4 µm³ volume, 997 mitochondria were visualized, giving a relative concentration of 0.36 mitochondria/µm³ (vs. 0.10 for brain), agreeing with previous observations.
evaluation: Claims C103-C112 provide comprehensive structural characterization of heart tissue with quantitative measurements of sarcomere length, mitochondrial density, and tissue volume. The mitochondrial concentration (C111) is validated by comparison to prior work (C112). The use of fixation (C103-C104) is justified for preserving tissue integrity between sectioning and vitrification.

result: Resolution varied across samples despite similar acquisition parameters. Brain and HeLa cells (same software, angle, pixel size) showed different resolutions, reflecting the importance of focusing, astigmatism, and sample variability. R. rubrum and Vero cells (similar pixel size, identical software, imaging angle) showed twofold resolution difference favoring Vero cells. No resolution degradation was observed during data collection, even in longer runs (HeLa—500 slices).
evaluation: Claims C113-C115 document important observations about resolution variability and stability. The lack of resolution degradation over time (C115) is crucial for validating the technique's reliability. The sample-to-sample variability (C113-C114) is appropriately attributed to multiple factors beyond just acquisition parameters.

result: Lamellae of R. rubrum and RPE-1 cells were generated and imaged by SEM during fabrication and TEM after fabrication. Final milling steps for lamella preparation used lower currents (60 pA) than cryo-serial pFIB/SEM imaging (200 pA). SEM and TEM images demonstrated correlation of subcellular features, though physical differences exist due to the distinctive physics of the techniques (SEM images ~25 nm depth at surface, TEM images entire lamella thickness up to 300 nm). Photosynthetic vesicles were straightforwardly correlated between modalities, and fluorescence from chlorophyll was correlated with both pFIB/SEM and TEM images.
evaluation: Claims C116-C123 demonstrate the compatibility of serial pFIB/SEM with downstream cryo-ET workflows. The correlation between SEM, TEM, and fluorescence imaging (C118, C121-C122) is supported by figures. The explanation of physical differences between modalities (C119-C120) is appropriate and based on the fundamental physics of the techniques. The conclusion about suitability for correlative workflows (C123) is well-supported.

result: Charging artifacts occurred when the electron beam interacted with highly insulating substances, typically in lipid-rich regions (membranes, vesicles, myelin), manifesting as intense dark spots with asymmetric streaks. A computational approach was developed for charging artifact removal. Automated segmentation of charge centers achieved a 0.93 Dice coefficient score compared to manual segmentation, indicating little manual cleanup was required and suggesting full automation is possible. After charge removal, overall image resolution remained unchanged.
evaluation: Claims C124-C130 describe both the physical basis of charging (C124-C126) and a computational mitigation approach (C127-C130). The high Dice coefficient (C128) validates the automated segmentation accuracy, and the preservation of resolution after charge removal (C130) demonstrates the method does not introduce additional artifacts. The approach is practical and well-validated.

result: Automated segmentation of mitochondria in heart tissue using a U-Net++ model trained in SuRVos2 achieved a Dice score of 0.87 compared to manual segmentation. The percentage of ROI segmented by SuRVos2 (24%) largely agreed with manual segmentation (20%). However, component counts differed (15 by SuRVos2 after filtering vs. 23 manually), indicating additional work is needed to quantify errors. The results demonstrate that cryo-serial pFIB/SEM data can be segmented in an automated fashion.
evaluation: Claims C131-C135 provide quantitative validation of automated segmentation with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations. The Dice score of 0.87 (C132) indicates good agreement, and the volume percentage comparison (C133) provides additional validation. The discrepancy in component counts (C134) is honestly reported, and the conclusion (C135) is appropriately qualified as a baseline demonstration rather than a fully validated method.

result: All four gases tested (O, N, Ar, Xe) can produce smooth surfaces under some conditions. Nitrogen and oxygen showed large curtaining propensity while xenon and argon showed lower propensity. Monatomic gases are speculated to be less reactive at biological material surfaces and less prone to curtaining. pFIB milling is effective for both plunge-frozen cells and HPF mouse tissue, though higher curtaining was observed in brain and heart tissue, attributed to greater initial unevenness due to lumen, fascia, and supportive layers milling at different rates.
evaluation: Claims C141-C146 summarize the gas evaluation results with appropriate distinction between data-driven conclusions (C141-C142, C144-C145) and speculation (C143). The observation of higher curtaining in tissue (C145) is explained by structural complexity. The suggestion for future exploration of coating approaches (C146) is supported by citation and is a reasonable direction for improvement.

result: Diatomic gases (O, N) led to double images with high automation failure rates (>80% vs. <10% for argon), requiring more manual operation. Oxygen plasma on resin-embedded samples has been reported as effective, but success rates were not reported. Argon and xenon have similarly low curtaining propensity at low current, making both strong candidates for this workflow. At high currents, argon performed better than xenon with reduced curtaining score and visual lack of curtains.
evaluation: Claims C147-C150 provide practical guidance for gas selection based on quantitative failure rates (C147) and curtaining performance (C149-C150). The citation to prior work with oxygen (C148) appropriately notes the limitation of unreported success rates. The conclusion favoring argon and xenon (C149) with argon preferred at high currents (C150) is well-supported by the data.

result: Prior work demonstrated pFIB lamella fabrication for cryo-ET, but milling with Ar plasma (30 kV, 60 pA) adversely affected ribosome resolution within ~45 nm of the surface despite smooth surfaces, attributed to argon ion damage. For serial pFIB/SEM, argon wattage is twofold higher than lamella polishing (200 pA at 20 kV vs. 50 pA at 30 kV). Damage would be expected to increase with current, though this is not established. Comparing Vero (nitrogen) and HeLa (argon) cells, nitrogen showed higher resolution. Damage may depend on plasma type, not simply current, and may not correlate with curtaining, but further investigation is required.
evaluation: Claims C151-C158 raise important concerns about potential damage from plasma milling, supported by citation to prior work (C151-C153). However, the relationship between curtaining, damage, and plasma type remains speculative (C156, C158). The observation that nitrogen showed higher resolution than argon (C157) is intriguing but based on limited comparison. The conclusion that damage may not correlate with curtaining (C154) is important but requires further investigation as acknowledged in C158.

result: The greatest SEM dose employed was under 10⁻² e⁻/Å² over the whole scanned image, lower than doses used during cryo-ET imaging. SEM-induced damage would be expected to be confined to the interaction depth (<50 nm), contained within the same volume as FIB damage (~45 nm from the surface).
evaluation: Claims C159-C161 provide quantitative dose measurements (C159) with appropriate comparison to cryo-ET (C160) supported by citation. The inference about damage confinement (C161) is reasonable based on electron interaction depth, though it is appropriately qualified as an expectation rather than a direct measurement.

result: Using low current, 50 nm layers were reliably ablated in a highly controlled manner. The absolute beam spot size is not necessarily the limiting factor for milling resolution—fine beam control, careful milling box placement, and steep beam profile can enable thinner slices than beam diameter. For plasma ion beams, thinner layer ablation is expected to be possible. The ideal milling step would match SEM electron penetration depth (20-30 nm), though this varies by sample. 50 nm was chosen as a compromise since smaller steps require more time and potentially introduce cumulative electron damage. No obvious vertical discontinuities from excessive electron dose were noticed.
evaluation: Claims C162-C168 provide a comprehensive discussion of milling resolution and parameter selection. The demonstration of controlled 50 nm milling (C162) is data-driven. The discussion of factors beyond beam spot size (C163) is well-reasoned, and the expectation of thinner layer capability (C164) is appropriately qualified as speculation. The rationale for 50 nm step size (C165-C167) is well-justified with citation, and the absence of dose-related artifacts (C168) validates the chosen parameters.

result: The rate-limiting step in the automated workflow was SEM imaging (6-7 min) with milling taking ~30 s on average. Using a faster-milling plasma at low power would have no significant improvement in overall time. Increasing SEM speed would be extremely beneficial for analyzing larger volumes. Scanning multiple lines concomitantly and/or software solutions would enable larger volume analysis and improve integration into other pipelines.
evaluation: Claims C169-C172 provide quantitative timing information (C169) leading to logical conclusions about workflow optimization (C170-C171). The suggestion for improving SEM speed through hardware or software approaches (C172) is supported by citation and represents a practical direction for future development.

result: Cryo-serial pFIB/SEM image quality was excellent even with sub-optimal geometry. Pixel size is critical for resolution. Patch size was maintained at 256×256 for all pixel sizes in FRC analysis, which may lead to more optimistic resolution estimates. Nonetheless, observation of macromolecular assemblies is consistent with calculated resolution better than 50 nm. By imaging 500 slices from HeLa cells, NPCs and centrioles were identified, indicating prophase but without spindle microtubules. In Vero cells, mitochondrial networks were delineated and ER-organelle contacts quantified. In brain tissue, complete synapses with pre-synaptic vesicles, myelin sheaths, and cell-cell interactions were visualized. Previous studies demonstrated SEM applicability to subcellular structures, but the current approach identified large macromolecular complexes even within tissues, representing significant improvement.
evaluation: Claims C173-C182 provide a comprehensive summary of imaging capabilities with appropriate acknowledgment of limitations (C175). The biological observations across different sample types (C177-C180) are well-documented with quantitative details. The comparison to prior work (C181-C182) appropriately contextualizes the advance, though the claim of 'significant improvement' could benefit from more specific comparison metrics.

result: Serial pFIB/SEM images could be correlated with fluorescence and TEM images, showing promise for correlative workflows. For targeting specific ROIs, lower-resolution SEM imaging may be possible and would increase throughput. The consequence of highest milling currents on TEM imaging quality has yet to be determined. Devitrification was not observed in mammalian cells or bacteria, though poor vitrification was observed in media surrounding bacteria, resulting from sample preparation. Sample charging was observed in all samples, most severe on lipid-rich regions. A software mitigation approach reduced charging effects on surrounding data but could not recover lost information. Preventing or reducing charging during acquisition would be preferable.
evaluation: Claims C183-C191 provide an honest assessment of both capabilities and limitations. The demonstration of correlative imaging (C183) is supported by data. The speculation about lower-resolution targeting (C184) and the acknowledgment of unknown effects at highest currents (C185) are appropriately qualified. The observations about vitrification quality (C186-C188) and charging (C189-C191) are data-driven with appropriate acknowledgment that prevention would be preferable to post-processing mitigation.

result: Automated machine learning segmentation of serial pFIB/SEM data achieved a Dice score of 0.87, largely agreeing with manual segmentation but less accurate where artifacts like charging were present. Enhanced contrast from perpendicular imaging paired with post-processing charge removal enabled automated volume segmentation. Serial pFIB/SEM can be utilized to provide quantitative information on subcellular organization within tissues.
evaluation: Claims C192-C195 demonstrate the feasibility of automated analysis with quantitative validation (C192) and appropriate acknowledgment of limitations (C193). The connection between imaging improvements and segmentation capability (C194) is logical, and the conclusion about quantitative tissue analysis (C195) is well-supported by the demonstrated examples.

result: Systematic comparison of Chlamydia-infected cells showed clear improvements in ultrastructure definition when imaging perpendicular to the surface. The quality difference was reduced but not eliminated by manual optimization of working distance. Both mature and developing chromatophores were segmented in R. rubrum. Unstained (but fixed) mouse heart was imaged with Z-disc to Z-disc distance measured as ~1.68 µm, likely demonstrating post-mortem sarcomere contraction rather than diastole (typical in vivo length ~1.7-2.3 µm). Images allowed accurate assessment of mitochondrial density and quantitative comparison with brain tissue. The ability to visualize protein assemblies and ultrastructure in vitrified unstained tissue with laboratory-based equipment has potential applications in pathology.
evaluation: Claims C196-C202 provide a comprehensive summary of biological applications with appropriate interpretation of observations. The sarcomere length measurement (C199-C200) is well-contextualized with citation, and the interpretation of post-mortem contraction is more likely than diastole. The quantitative comparison between tissues (C201) demonstrates the technique's analytical capabilities. The speculation about pathology applications (C202) is reasonable but appropriately qualified as potential.

result: Cryo-serial pFIB/SEM is a useful addition to the structural biology toolbox, accurately determining biological ultrastructural arrangements from simple bacteria to complex tissue. The approach can generate 3D maps of biological materials and has several key advantages: it is highly controllable, relatively rapid, can be done in a laboratory, and is compatible with subsequent imaging modalities.
evaluation: Claims C203-C206 provide an appropriate summary of the technique's capabilities and advantages. The demonstration across diverse sample types (C204) is well-supported by the presented data. The listed advantages (C206) are validated by the experimental results, including automation, timing measurements, and correlative imaging demonstrations.

result: The introduction establishes the context for cryo-serial pFIB/SEM by describing the capabilities and limitations of serial FIB/SEM (C1-C3), the requirements and challenges of cryo-ET (C7-C8, C12-C13), current approaches to lamella preparation (C9-C11), alternatives to cryo-CLEM (C14-C17), and the advantages of plasma FIB sources (C19-C21). The challenges of imaging native biological contrast are explained (C22-C24), along with strategies for reducing charging (C25-C26). The study evaluated different plasma gases and developed an automated workflow, achieving 20-50 nm resolution across bacteria, cells, and tissue, with specific biological observations in each sample type (C27-C33).
evaluation: Claims C1-C33 provide comprehensive background supported by appropriate citations and establish the rationale for the study. The description of current methods and their limitations (C5-C6, C12-C13, C16-C17, C22-C24) is well-documented. The summary of results (C27-C33) accurately reflects the experimental findings presented in detail elsewhere. This is primarily contextual and methodological framing rather than novel results.
